title: Combined tDCS and tcVNS for Anxiety and Depression: A Pilot Study Revealing Age- and Severity-Dependent Therapeutic Responses
content: Anxiety and depressive disorders are among the leading causes of disability worldwide, yet current treatments remain limited by modest efficacy and restricted accessibility; non-invasive neuromodulation techniques as transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) and transcutaneous cervical vagus nerve stimulation (tcVNS) have emerged as promising alternatives whose combination may produce synergistic clinical effects. Methods: This proof-of-concept pilot study evaluated the feasibility, tolerability, and preliminary clinical effects of a combined tDCS and tcVNS protocol in 12 adults (Mage = 54.75 ± 17.47 years) with clinically significant anxiety and depressive symptoms; participants received 10 consecutive sessions of anodal tDCS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (2 mA, 20 min) followed by tcVNS with PEMF, with symptoms assessed using the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) and pre–post comparisons performed via the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results: Significant reductions were observed for both outcomes: BAI scores decreased by 52.0% (Z = −3.059, p &lt; .001, r = .883) and BDI scores by 55.9% (Z = −3.059, p &lt; .001, r = .883); BDI remission rates rose from 8.3% to 83.3%, and no adverse events were reported. Standard clinical response rates (≥ 50% score reduction from baseline) were achieved by 50.0% of participants for depression (BDI) and 41.7% for anxiety (BAI), with 25.0% demonstrating concurrent dual response on both measures. A stratification into distinct response profile revealed that high responders presented with an older age profile (M = 63.33 ± 9.87 years vs. 51.89 ± 18.94 years), more pronounced baseline anxiety (M = 37.67 ± 3.06 vs. 31.67 ± 9.29), and higher baseline depression (M = 24.67 ± 5.51 vs. 21.56 ± 6.35). Conclusion: Combined tDCS and tcVNS appears feasible, well tolerated, and associated with substantial symptom reductions, warranting further investigation in adequately powered randomized sham-controlled trials.
